world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Li, Paul Jen-kuei (1973) Rukai Structure (316pp grammar); Zeitoun, Elizabeth (2007) A Grammar of Mantauran (Rukai) (569pp); Hsin (2000) Aspects of Maga Rukai Phonology — none reachable online

new_statements.quote: Every content word in Rukai is stressed on the last syllable, e.g. [bavá] 'wine', [tuLú] 'three', [taLagí] 'friend'. This can be accounted for by a phonological rule that assigns stress to the final syllable of a word (see 3.9). There are two general types of exceptions to the stress rule. All interrogative words receive a stress on the penultimate syllable, e.g. [ʔíya] 'how much' (vs. [ʔiyá] 'do'), [mikakúwa] 'how', [manɨ́ma] 'what', [anɨ́a] 'who', [lwíga] 'when (future)', [kwíga] 'when (past)', [ínu] 'where'. These have to be treated as lexical exceptions. [...] The monosyllabic articles [ka], [sa], [ku] and [ki] (cf. 4.2.2.2) are also exceptions in that they do not bear stress. One further exception: [kuíya] 'there (far)'.
new_statements.citation: Li, Paul Jen-kuei. 1973. Rukai Structure. Institute of History and Philology Special Publications No. 64. Taipei: Academia Sinica.
new_statements.locator: Section 2.5 'Stress', p. 21 (PDF page 33 of the Academia Sinica IL scan); see also sec. 2.6 p. 22 and sec. 3.5 p. 52
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Tanan (Taromak) dialect described by Li, stress falls on the final syllable of every content word, assigned by rule; the final syllable is counted without the optional 'echo vowel' that can follow a word-final consonant (Li leaves echo vowels out of underlying forms precisely so that stress is predictable and final; if they are counted, consonant-final words surface as penult-stressed). Interrogative words are lexically marked for penultimate stress; the monosyllabic articles are unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Interrogatives (ʔíya 'how much', mikakúwa 'how', manɨ́ma 'what', anɨ́a 'who', lwíga/kwíga 'when', ínu 'where') take penultimate stress as lexical exceptions; articles ka, sa, ku, ki bear no stress; kuíya 'there (far)'; apparent pairs like [taí] 'taro' vs [tái] 'family' are resolved as tai vs tay (final /y, w/) rather than as stress exceptions (p. 22). Li 1977: 8, 26 (same author) later calls stress phonemic in all dialects except Mantauran and only 'mostly' final in Tanan; Blust 2013: 173, 666-667 lists cross-dialect stress disagreements (Tanan/Tona abó vs Budai ábo 'ash').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (content words in citation/isolation); Li's rule applies to the phonological word as represented without echo vowels. Dialect-specific: Tanan. Other dialects per Li 1977 (pp. 8, 26, 85-86): Budai, Tona, Maga, Labuan mostly penultimate with contrastive (phonemic) stress; Mantauran non-phonemic, on the first syllable of the stem.
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1973 describes the Tanan (Taromak/Tarumak) dialect of Taitung, Glottolog dialect tana1287 (main informant Te-tz'u Lin, p. 10). Stress placement is dialect-dependent in Rukai: Li 1977 (pp. 8, 26, 85-86) states stress is phonemic in all dialects except Mantauran (mant1271, stem-initial), mostly final in Tanan (if echo vowels are omitted) but mostly penultimate in Budai (buda1252), Tona (tona1238), Maga (maga1265) and Labuan (labu1252); Blust 2013: 173, 666-667 confirms contrastive, cross-dialectally disagreeing stress. A language-level reading for ruka1240 should therefore be flagged as dialect-specific (Tanan = fixed-final by rule; Budai etc. = mostly penult, lexically contrastive).

sources.locator: Section 2.5 'Stress', p. 21 (PDF page 33 of the Academia Sinica IL scan); see also sec. 2.6 p. 22 and sec. 3.5 p. 52
sources.note: Sec. 2.5 'Stress' (p. 21): every content word is stressed on the last syllable, by a phonological rule assigning stress to the final syllable; exceptions: interrogatives take penultimate stress (lexical exceptions), monosyllabic articles ka/sa/ku/ki are unstressed, plus [kuíya] 'there (far)'. Sec. 2.6 (p. 22) resolves [taí] 'taro' vs [tái] 'family' as tai vs tay rather than as stress/length exceptions. Sec. 3.5 (p. 52): leaving optional final echo vowels out of underlying forms 'makes stress more predictable: stress mostly falls on the final syllable'. Dialect = Tanan (Taromak), p. 7.

sources.note: p. 173: 'Stress is phonemic in Kanakanabu, and in all dialects of Rukai except Mantauran, but stress contrasts in cognate morphemes differ sufficiently between these languages that Li (1977b) omitted contrastive stress in his reconstruction of Proto Rukai phonology.' pp. 666-667: 'Several Rukai dialects have contrastive stress, but they often disagree' — Tanan/Tona abó vs Budai ábo 'ash', etc.; 'The history of stress in Rukai remains to be worked out.' p. 565: Ross 1992 claimed Budai oxytones reflect PAN contrastive stress; Blust 1997d rejects this. p. 567: Wolff 1991 'Rukai stress furnishes…

sources.note: p. 8: 'Stress is phonemic in all the dialects except Mantauran, in which it falls on the first syllable of a stem. Stress would be more nearly predictable if the final echo vowels are not represented in the phonemic transcriptions, particularly in the dialect of Tanan (see Li 1973: 51-55).' p. 26: in Tanan stress is 'mostly in the final syllable' if echo vowels are not written; 'stress mostly falls on the penult in the other dialects'. p. 7 n. 2: treating long vowels as geminates in Maga makes 'stress... more regular on the penult (see Li 1975b)'.
